e: Card players’ term: keeping your hands above the board (table) so you can’t cheat.
t: Hands above the card table: no cheating underneath.
« Être pris d’amok »: a frenzied, uncontrolled rampage.
Same as « animosité ».
Apex predator = top of the food chain.
Same as « avarice »: L’Avare.

e: From the animal; badger-baiting set dogs to harass a badger in its burrow.
t: Dogs pestering a badger in its hole: badgering your manager for an answer.
« Un sourire béat »: blessed (béatitude).

e: From become in the sense “to suit” (Old English becuman).
t: A dress that becomes you = « qui te va bien ».
Bellum = war: « belliqueux ».

m: Very pale, thin or bony, like a corpse.
t: Same as « cadavérique ».

e: Latin cardinalis, from cardo (hinge). The point on which everything turns.
t: The hinge everything turns on: cardinal sins, cardinal points.

m: Something that causes or speeds up a change.
t: Same as « catalyseur ».

m: A person with excessive or prejudiced loyalty to their group.
e: French chauvin, after Nicolas Chauvin, a probably legendary, fanatically loyal Napoleonic soldier.
t: Nicolas Chauvin and his blind patriotism. Male chauvinist = « macho ».

m: To restrain or stop; a restraint.
e: Old French eschec (check in chess), from Persian shāh (king). The king is stopped.
t: Échec au roi! Checks and balances = « contre-pouvoirs ».

m: Marked by changes of fortune, often including bad episodes.
e: From the chessboard pattern (Old French eschequier, chessboard).
t: A chessboard of black and white squares: a checkered past.
An argument that compels you (cogere). Une raison cogente is rare in French.
Same as « contrit ».

m: To confirm or give support to.
t: Same as « corroborer »: strong as oak.
Un-sacred: « profaner une tombe ».
Same as « disparate ».

m: Straying from the proper course; wandering.
t: A knight-errant wanders; an errant child strays.
Same as « exhorter ».

m: Making a fault seem less serious.
t: Circonstances atténuantes = extenuating circumstances: thinning the guilt.

e: From the animal, Old French furet, used to hunt rabbits out of burrows.
t: « Fureter » like un furet: ferreting out the truth.

e: Old English flēos (sheep’s wool). To shear someone of their money.
t: Shearing a sheep: « se faire plumer / tondre ».

m: Having plenty of money; also level with.
e: Of uncertain origin; “flush with money” from the idea of being full to overflowing.
f: en fonds; à fleur de, de niveau
t: A river in flood is flush: flush with cash.

e: From an old exclamation of joy, hey-day! (16th c.).
t: Shouting « hey! » in your best years.

e: From hotchpotch, French hochepot, a stew of mixed ingredients.
t: Hochepot, a Flemish stew: everything thrown in.
It doesn’t matter: that’s immaterial.

m: A factor difficult or impossible to assess.
t: « Les impondérables »: what can’t be weighed.

m: A military group ruling after seizing power.
t: « La junte militaire ».
Same as « lassitude »: las.
Straight from « mêlée », even in rugby.
Molière’s « Le Misanthrope », Alceste.

e: Latin momentum (movement, weight), from movere. A weight that tips the scale.
t: Momentum tips the balance: a decision of great moment.
Paucus = few (peu).

m: A very small or inadequate amount of money.
e: Old French pitance (a monk’s ration given out of piety), from pitié.
t: « Une maigre pitance ».

m: Taken to prevent an anticipated event.
t: A preemptive strike: acting before the other side does.
Pugnus = poing: « pugnace ».

e: Probably from raff (heap, rubbish), influenced by raft (a floating mass of logs).
t: A raft of logs floating together: a raft of new rules.
« Repu » after a feast: replete with.

m: Making a show of moral superiority.
t: Fake saintliness: « des airs de sainte nitouche ».

m: Optimistic, especially in a difficult situation.
e: Latin sanguineus (bloody). In humour theory, blood made people cheerful.
t: Ruddy-cheeked and cheerful: a sanguine temperament. Not bloodthirsty.
« Scintillant »: sparkling conversation.

e: Old English styrtan (to leap up). The jump came before the begin sense.
t: To wake with a start = « se réveiller en sursaut ».

m: To stop or restrict a flow.
t: Stem the bleeding, stem the tide: « endiguer ».

m: Not right or reasonable; shockingly unfair.
t: Something no conscience could accept.

e: Latin vicarius (substitute), from vicis (change, turn), as in vicar and vice-president.
t: Living through your kids = « vivre par procuration ».

m: A domineering, violent or bad-tempered woman.
t: Same as « virago ».

m: To grow larger (wax and wane); to speak in a certain way.
t: The moon waxes and wanes: grows and shrinks. Wax lyrical = devenir lyrique.
